A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SRFT study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v5.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-4.1 fine-tuning and interrogation experiments, Claude prefill comparisons, robustness analyses, and capability evaluations.

after.justification: v5 retains these original results and adds training-data ablations, held-out validation, and instruction-hierarchy compliance experiments.

M1.justification: The primary SRFT procedure retains GPT-4.1, the 770 two-turn training examples, and the interrogation procedure. v5 explicitly documents training both assistant turns, including false first answers; this clarifies the setup rather than establishes an algorithm change. The additional training variants serve as experimental ablations.

E1.justification: v5 substantially expands auxiliary coverage with a general instruction-hierarchy conflict task, general instruction-tuning data for mixing, and difficult HLE questions used to train admissions under mistaken beliefs. The four stealth tasks and existing capability benchmarks remain; the new held-out factual-QA validation alone does not constitute new task coverage.

E2.justification: The original GPT-4.1, monitor, prefill, and Claude comparisons remain. v5 adds comparisons within the SRFT family, including turn2-only and no-turn2 baselines, a prompted-false-answer variant, and belief-aligned versus ground-truth-aligned training variants (Figures 4–5 and Appendix A.2).

E3.justification: New protocols include comparing ablations on common GPT-4.1 trajectories, validating 400 held-out questions and 800 admissions, and evaluating 247 instruction conflicts across eight types. v5 also specifies HLE filtering and controlled data-mixing and admission-corruption conditions. The original stealth-task sampling and principal metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendices A.2, H, and L.1 add substantial tests of training-turn necessity, model belief versus ground truth, benign-data mixing, inaccurate admissions, and instruction-hierarchy side effects. Earlier decoy, auditing-only, and system-prompt analyses remain, including the system-prompt analysis relocated to Appendix K.

E5.justification: v5 first specifies fine-tuning seed 42. Existing interrogation repetition counts and Wilson interval, bootstrap interval, and standard-error reporting practices are retained. The added seed disclosure does not establish additional training runs or rerunning the original experiments.

E6.justification: The headline F1 of 0.98 and 28–100% elicitation results remain unchanged. Substantial new outcomes include zero elicitation for turn2-only training, 61% factual-QA and 96% admission accuracy for SRFT in held-out validation, and hierarchy compliance of 72% for GPT-4.1 versus 61% for SRFT. Figures 5, 17, and 18 additionally report belief-target, mixing, and contamination results.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The F1 and elicitation metric definitions are retained. The new explanations and empirical selection rules do not introduce a formal theory.

C1.justification: v5 refines the central contribution to generalization from admissions of on-policy mistakes. Its abstract and conclusion explicitly describe training models to make factual errors and then confess them. The principal detection, elicitation, and decoy-robustness claims remain.

C2.justification: v5 adds substantive explanations involving on-policy errors, stronger training updates, and admissions aligned with model belief. It also identifies weakened instruction-hierarchy compliance as a possible contributor to disclosure and explicitly acknowledges that the evaluation confounds this with honesty. These materially qualify the earlier interpretation.

D1.justification: v5 clarifies assistant-message weighting and which turns receive training, documents the new ablation recipes, and replaces the anonymized repository pointer with a named GitHub repository. These improve documentation without proving changes to the original implementation. The instruction-tuning data source remains unresolved as '(?)' in Appendix H.1.

R1.justification: v5 removes the related-work paragraph on unexpected fine-tuning generalization and its references to Betley et al. on emergent misalignment, He et al. on benign data breaking safety, and Qi et al. on fine-tuning compromising safety. The broader positioning around auditing, probing, steering, and introspection remains.

P1.justification: v5 regroups the methods subsections, condenses several passages, repairs incomplete wording, and moves the detailed system-prompt analysis into Appendix K. Appendices are reorganized, but much of the introduction, principal results, and retained appendix text remains verbatim or lightly edited.

P2.justification: v5 adds multi-panel ablation, validation, and hierarchy-compliance figures; relocates the system-prompt figure; and redraws the capability plots with explicit numerical labels and revised axes and ordering. It also corrects the training-example illustration and caption. This substantially expands and revises the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens the paper by testing which training ingredients support generalization and examining instruction-hierarchy weakening as an alternative explanation, gaps left largely untested in v1. Clearer training documentation and explicit limitations make the retained headline results easier to interpret. The hierarchy confound remains unresolved, and missing data provenance and small prose–figure discrepancies limit precision, but the added controls and qualifications provide a substantial net improvement.
